idiom_name: final class DirView: Dir with hand-written mediated members
implementation_notes: Swift has no general dynamic interception: a membrane is a type that conforms to the same protocol and implements every mediated member by hand, holding the wrapped instance and wrapping arguments and results by hand - the delegation model the Swift book describes for protocols. On Darwin platforms the Objective-C runtime still offers NSProxy, a root class whose only purpose is to forward unknown messages, but it works only for @objc message dispatch and does not exist on Swift for Linux. For member-level forwarding Swift 4.2 added @dynamicMemberLookup (SE-0195), which turns member access on the wrapper into a subscript call; it cannot intercept a method called on a value it returns, so it is a convenience, not a mediation hook. This explicit form is the one to use whenever calls must actually be mediated.
pitfalls: Conformance catches protocol growth at compile time, but generic and Any payloads bypass the wrapper: an API that accepts Any or a generic parameter hands the raw value through unless the membrane is reflected in the types.
NSProxy is only available where the Objective-C runtime is and only for @objc protocols; a design that relies on it is platform-bound and cannot be the default.

Protocol witness tables dispatch statically: if the wrapper is passed as the concrete type or inlined, calls still hit the wrapper's methods, but a protocol extension method that uses Self or exists only in an extension can execute without the wrapper's overrides.

variants.name: @dynamicMemberLookup forwarding wrapper
variants.implementation_notes: SE-0195 lets a wrapper turn unknown member accesses into subscript calls: a type marked @dynamicMemberLookup implements subscript(dynamicMember:) and the compiler rewrites `wrapper.member` (reads, writes and inout uses) into that subscript, so the membrane can route member access through one place (swift-evolution proposal 0195). It covers member selection only - a call on the value it returns runs on that value, so arguments and results of methods must still be wrapped by the returned expressions themselves; use it to forward a property surface onto a wrapped object while keeping the membrane's checks, and keep the explicit protocol wrapper for call-level mediation.
pitfalls: Key paths are resolved at compile time: the subscript only sees key paths, so members not expressible as WritableKeyPath (methods, throwing accessors, metatypes) cannot be forwarded through it.

The subscript must not read through a strong reference to the wrapper while writing through the raw object, or the membrane changes value semantics for inout uses; revoked writes must fail loudly rather than silently no-op.
dynamicMemberLookup is on by default in Swift 5 and only forwards member access - a returned object is unwrapped unless the subscript itself wraps it, so forgetting the wrap reopens the graph.
